title: Key points
items: A handshake agrees a secret key
Encryption costs a round trip, little else
A certificate is a signed ID card for a site

say: three parts: how the handshake works, where the extra time goes, and what a certificate actually is.
first the browser says hello and sends its half of a key exchange.
the server answers with its certificate and its own half.
both sides combine the halves into the same secret key, without ever sending it.
from then on everything between them is encrypted with that key.
it's slower mostly because of that handshake: an extra round trip before the first byte, less with newer TLS.
the encryption itself is cheap on modern chips, and returning visitors can resume the session.
a certificate is a signed statement that this key belongs to this site, vouched for by a chain of authorities your device trusts.
it names the site, who signed it, when it expires and the site's public key.
so a quick handshake buys you a private, verified connection for the cost of one round trip.
